name: Marco Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for any side. Everything here is confidential. Can you take me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco Kowalski, forty-three. On Saturdays I meet builders at Riverbend Tax, then spend Monday checking what I missed in their invoices. I did a bachelor's in accounting before years keeping books for a building co-op, but tax returns are newer to me, so I'm a junior and my supervisor catches plenty. I never use the firm's AI sorter; the blue tick sheet is still beside my keyboard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work do you like, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like hearing why a builder bought something rather than guessing from a line on paper. I dislike being slower on unfamiliar tax codes. Riverbend pays me above the usual rate because it struggles to staff Saturday client appointments. My partner Salma works at the library, our children are seven and twelve, and we have a mortgage with ten months of expenses saved. There are plenty of firms nearby if I need to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small improvement would be fine with me. The practice has an AI sorter, but I use the handwritten tick sheet and let someone else work the new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients their tax return still needs a person who will answer the phone. I'd ask the union branch to make sure faster sorting means a fair workload, not more files pushed onto juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our household would be secure enough in that world. I'm forty-three and junior at Riverbend Tax because construction accounts are different from the co-op books I used to keep. The firm pays me above the usual rate for Saturday client appointments, Salma has a library wage, and we have ten months of expenses saved with plenty of firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the Saturday appointments and my supervisor's check on complicated building expenses. I'd keep the monthly savings transfer of three hundred running. In the first year of a plateau, I'd ask the branch to put a limit on return files assigned during the Saturday shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my mortgage and wages. I'm not quick on tax codes yet, but I can learn on a normal workday without a cliff under us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake changed your checklist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A roofer brought a receipt for a ladder and a roof repair on the same bill. I nearly entered both as equipment before my supervisor stopped me. My blue tax checklist now has a note about mixed invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union see about Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the branch three Saturdays where the file queue ran past the advertised hours. If the partners want more returns, they should pay for another person or more time. I won't ask the children to wait in a car park while I finish a queue.

say: I would keep **human answers** behind every signed tax return a builder receives.
I would ask for a fair **Saturday workload**.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** protects the mortgage if a Saturday appointment is cancelled.
A high **Saturday rate** supports us despite my junior tax skills.
do: Ask the **union branch** for a Saturday file limit.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages and the mortgage.
S0.quote: My blue tax checklist now has a note about mixed invoices.
fieldNote: The **Saturday premium** explains higher pay without implying senior tax skill.
A **ten-month reserve** and two wages make the plateau manageable despite his dislike of AI tools.

steps.text: Keep Saturday client appointments and supervisor review of building expenses
Transfer three hundred monthly into savings
Ask union branch for limit on Saturday return files

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking and answering customers make up most of the junior desk. If a system takes those, the Saturday premium could vanish before my mortgage does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say staff should see the staffing plan and be paid to retrain. I'd tell the partners that saving time is no excuse to put every awkward return on one junior without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own paid Saturday hours could be reduced, perhaps one shift a month. Salma's library wage and ten months saved give us time, and there are many firms nearby, but that higher rate is a real part of our household income. I still struggle with unfamiliar tax cases and do not use AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take my last eight Saturday rotas to the union branch and ask for a staffing meeting before any change. I'd ask my supervisor for paid time to practice mixed construction invoices, using the old files I got wrong. If the premium shift disappears, I'd apply for a funded builders' co-op accounts post only if its advertised wage covers our mortgage and its start date is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing part of my wage, though I am not trapped. A bank statement can look healthy and still hide how much one shift pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would losing Saturdays have any upside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our younger son plays club football on Saturdays, and I miss enough matches already. If the premium shift goes, I would see more of him, but we would still need to replace the pay. I won't call a cut a family benefit unless the mortgage is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the co-op post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The co-op would need to show an actual payroll vacancy, not a friendly offer from an old colleague. I'd ask for the salary, weekend hours and start date in writing. If those do not fit childcare and the mortgage, I stay at Riverbend while looking.

say: I would demand a **staffing meeting** before the partners change paid Saturday hours.
I would seek **paid practice** on harder returns.
think: My **Saturday premium** could shrink even if my weekday tax files remain.
Ten months saved and **nearby firms** give me some control.
do: Bring **eight rotas** to the union branch.
Practice **mixed invoices** with a supervisor in paid time.
Seek **posted funded co-op work** after Saturday loss, requiring written mortgage-covering pay, confirmed pickup and start; otherwise keep Riverbend pay while searching.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing premium pay.
S1.quote: I won't call a cut a family benefit unless the mortgage is covered.
fieldNote: **Premium Saturday pay** makes a partial hour cut material even with strong savings.
The **co-op fallback** requires a payroll vacancy, mortgage-covering wage, childcare-compatible hours and a confirmed start.

steps.text: Bring eight Saturday rotas to union staffing meeting
Practice mixed invoices if supervisor grants paid time
Seek posted funded co-op role after Saturday loss only with written mortgage-covering pay and confirmed start
Require confirmed school pickup; otherwise keep current pay while searching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is too soon to turn a whole office into something else. A machine that does the thinking cheaply could take the building returns and my client calls together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for legal notice, income support and a union meeting before layoffs. I'd tell friends that a family with savings should not be the only family able to wait for a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior accounting job to go in the first year after full AGI arrives in 2028. My desk work is thinking work, so robots around 2031 do not give me more time. Ten months saved and many local firms help, but those firms may lose the same tax work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying extra on the mortgage this month and hold the four hundred in our emergency account. I'd apply for the open library procurement post if it is funded, pays enough and has hours that let me collect the children. In the first year after 2028, if Riverbend ends my job, I'd claim wage support and use savings for the regular mortgage while seeking work outside tax preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect to lose a good wage in a crowded market. The savings make a plan possible, but I would still lie awake counting months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner increase her hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Salma would keep the library shifts she already has, but there are no promised extra hours. I'd show her the exact reserve and the school pickup times before applying elsewhere. We should not budget an overtime shift that nobody has offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which conditions decide the procurement job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The procurement post needs a funded salary and a written start date before I resign. I'd check the pickup schedule with Salma, because an evening shift can cost us childcare. If the vacancy closes, I stay at Riverbend until the decision is made.

say: I would seek **notice and income support** for displaced workers.
I would demand a **union meeting** before cuts.
think: My **desk job** may end soon after 2028 despite a well-paid Saturday client rota.
Ten months saved cannot make a **tax-wide shock** harmless.
do: Hold **four hundred monthly** instead of extra mortgage payments.
Apply for **funded procurement work** with adequate salary and pickup hours; retain current pay until written start or if vacancy closes.
Claim **wage support** after dismissal, covering regular mortgage from savings while seeking work outside tax.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing a high wage.
S2.quote: We should not budget an overtime shift that nobody has offered.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his returns and client calls in 2028; later robots offer no delay.
The **procurement fallback** has funding, salary, start-date and school-pickup conditions.

steps.text: Hold four hundred monthly in cash instead of extra mortgage payments
Apply for funded procurement with adequate salary and pickup hours; require written start before resigning
Keep current pay if procurement closes; search outside tax after dismissal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me look at real jobs before making a move. I still would not take a course just because somebody tells me accountants need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the partners should publish which posts may go and fund people to move. I'd ask the union to bargain for paid supervised placements, not vouchers with no vacancy attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could return to the builders' co-op in a client records role, but its accounts desk would also face thinking AI in 2031. I would only move if the co-op needed someone to help members untangle real problems and offered a funded wage. Robots in 2034 do not extend my current return job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in the co-op member-advice course this year if Riverbend pays the five-hundred fee and gives paid study hours. I'd handle one real member dispute under supervision if the co-op agrees and releases me for a paid day. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends, I'd apply for a funded member-adviser vacancy only if salary and school-pickup hours fit our mortgage and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have time to ask for proof. I would rather keep a paid job than collect certificates while our savings leak away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek firm funding with a strong cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five hundred would not ruin us, but the practice benefits from a service its clients might use. If the firm refuses the fee or paid hours, I would use free co-op seminars and keep my present wage. I would not call that the same as handling a case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the placement real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispute should involve a real member who agrees to my presence and a supervisor who corrects me. If it is only an online demonstration, I cannot tell whether I can do the job. I'd ask for written feedback before applying.

say: I would seek **published posts** and paid moves before tax return work disappears.
I would ask for **supervised placements** through the union.
think: A **member-advice role** might be a bridge, not permanent safety.
I need **funded wages** more than another certificate.
do: Enrol in **member-advice study** if firm funds fee and paid hours; otherwise keep current wage and use free sessions.
Handle a **real member dispute** if co-op grants paid supervision.
Apply after **2031 tax job loss** for funded advice work with mortgage-covering pay and pickup, obtaining written supervised-case feedback before applying.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to demand proof.
S3.quote: I would rather keep a paid job than collect certificates while our savings leak away.
fieldNote: **Firm-paid study** and a real supervised case are required before he treats member advice as a job route.
The **co-op move** remains conditional on funded pay and school-pickup hours after 2031.

steps.text: Enrol in member-advice course if firm funds fee and paid study
Handle real dispute if co-op grants paid supervised day
Keep current wage and use free co-op seminars if fee or paid time refused
Apply for funded adviser vacancy after 2031 tax job loss only with mortgage-covering pay and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in our children's lives. By 2036 they would be nearly grown, and I could build member-advice experience slowly if there is paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask employers to spread the savings through shorter weeks and paid moves rather than one abrupt redundancy round. I'd also support public training places for people who lack my household cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect tax returns to be mostly automated when thinking AI arrives in 2036. Member advice may exist, but I cannot call it safe until the co-op budgets a post. Robots around 2039 do not keep my desk work alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current Saturday client rota and ask the co-op next spring about a funded part-time member-advice place with paid supervision. I would move only if the published wage covers our mortgage, school pickup works and the start date is firm. In the first year after 2036, if my tax post ends, I'd take a funded co-op adviser vacancy if offered; otherwise I'd claim support and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. We can use ten years to make a careful choice while the children still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter would be twenty-two by then and our son seventeen. I hope the older one can choose her own work instead of feeling she has to rescue our mortgage. I would keep the reserve for us to carry our own risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op place is vague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the wage, the supervisor's name and the actual funded opening. If any of those are missing, I keep the Saturday job and use free member meetings to learn the work. A promise of a future place is not a payslip.

I would support **public training** for workers without savings.
think: My **return work** still faces AGI in 2036.
A **co-op adviser post** needs a budget and real wage.
do: Keep **Saturday clients** and attend free co-op meetings if no funded place opens.
Seek a **funded supervised co-op place** next spring; move only with mortgage-covering wage, confirmed pickup and start.
After **2036 tax job loss**, take a funded adviser vacancy; otherwise claim support while searching.
feel: I feel **uneasy** while planning a careful move.
S4.quote: A promise of a future place is not a payslip.
fieldNote: The **ten-year horizon** lets him explore member advice without risking current high pay prematurely.
The **funded opening** must carry a supervisor, mortgage-covering wage, workable school hours and firm start.

steps.text: Keep Saturday clients and attend free co-op meetings if no funded post opens

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my desk job and Saturday premium could go together. Notice, income support, paid supervised training and a funded vacancy with school-pickup hours would help. Savings buy us ten months, not a guarantee that local firms will keep tax staff. I want a real payroll number before I move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who covers the children when a 'new opportunity' starts at six in the evening. Salma's library hours are set, and my daughter still needs collecting. A new wage that creates an uncovered school pickup is not a workable offer.

headlineQuote: A new wage that creates an uncovered school pickup is not a workable offer.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Marco is a junior tax accountant after years keeping books for a building co-op.
His **accounting bachelor’s** and Saturday client premium bring high pay despite tax skills he is still learning.
He **never uses AI**, relying on a blue paper checklist and supervisor corrections.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and ten months saved give security, with plenty of firms nearby.
He favours **union bargaining** and funded work with childcare-compatible hours before leaving his current wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his desk role and Saturday premium together.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **notice**, income support, supervised paid training and a funded job that fits school pickup.
